title: Universities Should Not Ban Generative AI: Redesign Assessment Instead
artefact:
Calls to ban generative artificial intelligence from universities have grown louder since tools that draft essays and solve problems became freely available. The impulse is understandable. Academics worry that students will outsource their thinking, that grades will stop reflecting learning, and that the value of a degree will erode. Yet a blanket ban is the wrong response. It is unenforceable, it widens existing inequalities, and it ducks the real task, which is to redesign how we assess learning. Universities should permit generative AI under clear rules and rebuild assessment around what these tools cannot do well.

Consider enforcement first. A ban only works if violations can be detected, and detection is failing. Commercial classifiers that claim to spot AI-written text produce both false positives and false negatives at rates too high for academic penalties. Some have flagged work by non-native English speakers more often, raising a fairness problem of their own. A rule that cannot be applied consistently is not a rule; it is a lottery. Worse, an unenforceable ban punishes the honest. Students who comply forgo a tool their less scrupulous peers use undetected, so the policy rewards exactly the behaviour it means to stop.

Equity deepens the objection. Banning AI on university devices and networks does not remove it from students' lives; it removes it from the supervised, documented setting where staff could teach good practice. Wealthier students will still reach premium models at home. Students juggling jobs and caring duties, who could use AI to draft an outline at midnight, lose a genuine support. A ban therefore tends to hand an advantage to those already advantaged, the opposite of what most universities claim to want.

The strongest case for permitting AI, though, is educational. The skills graduates now need include framing a problem for a model, judging whether its output is correct, and revising it. These are not trivial. Evaluating a confident but wrong answer demands exactly the disciplinary knowledge a degree is supposed to build. A course that forbids AI prepares students for a workplace that no longer exists. One that teaches critical, supervised use builds judgement that transfers.

This educational point matters most in disciplines where the hard part has never been producing text but deciding whether the text is right. A law student must learn to spot the case a model has misread; a medical student must recognise when a plausible summary omits a contraindication; an engineering student must catch a calculation that is fluent and wrong. None of that judgement is built by pretending the tool does not exist. It is built by putting students in front of imperfect machine output and asking them to find the flaw, which is exactly the kind of exercise a thoughtful curriculum can set. A ban forecloses that teaching; supervised use enables it.

None of this means assessment can stay as it is. Here the critics are right: the unsupervised take-home essay, marked as a proxy for understanding, is now a weak instrument. The answer is to change the instrument, not to police the tool. Several redesigns work. Oral examinations, in which a student defends their reasoning, are hard to fake and reveal depth quickly. In-class writing under supervision tests composition directly. Project work assessed across drafts, with a short reflective account of how AI was used, rewards process rather than a single polished artefact. Assignments can be built around materials the model has not seen, such as data the student gathered, a local case, or last week's seminar discussion. Each shifts the target from a product a machine can generate to thinking a student must demonstrate.

A fair argument deserves its counterarguments. Three are serious. First, redesign costs money and time. Oral exams do not scale cheaply to a cohort of six hundred, and overstretched departments may lack the staff. This is real, and it means the transition must be funded and phased rather than demanded overnight. Second, allowing AI may let weak students coast while appearing competent, blurring the signal a degree sends to employers. That risk is genuine, which is precisely why supervised, AI-resistant components must anchor the grade. Third, some disciplines rest on foundational skills, such as mental arithmetic or basic proof, that must be built before a tool can safely assist. For those, restricting AI in early courses is defensible. The point is that these are arguments for selective, justified limits, not for a universal ban.

There is also a softer worry that constant access to fluent text will dull students' own voices. It might. But the same was said of calculators, spell-checkers, and the web, and the sensible response each time was to teach when the tool helps and when it gets in the way, while still requiring unaided performance where it matters. That is a curriculum question, answerable course by course, not a reason to wall off the technology entirely.

What, concretely, should a university do? It should set a clear default that AI use is permitted but must be disclosed, with disclosure norms that vary by assignment. It should fund a programme to redesign high-stakes assessment towards supervised and authentic tasks over two to three years. It should train staff to use AI as a teaching aid, for instance generating practice questions or worked counter-examples. And it should keep a small set of explicitly AI-free assessments where a skill must be demonstrated unaided, named as such so the rule is transparent.

A ban offers the comfort of a clear line and the appearance of resolve. But it cannot be enforced, it falls hardest on the students with the least, and it leaves the underlying weakness in assessment untouched. The harder path, redesigning how we measure learning, is also the honest one. It treats students as people we are preparing for the world as it is, and it puts the burden of adaptation where it belongs, on the institution rather than on a rule no one can keep.

valid: The essay's central remedy, redesigning assessment, is asserted more than costed. It claims orals and authentic tasks solve the problem but only gestures at the scale issue in a single sentence near the end. For a cohort of six hundred, oral exams are a serious logistical and financial commitment, and the piece never engages with how that is actually paid for. That gap weakens the argument's practicality.

Several empirical claims are stated without any citation. The assertion that AI detectors flag non-native speakers more often, and the claim about false-positive rates being too high for penalties, are presented as settled fact. They may well be true, but in an argumentative essay that leans on them as load-bearing evidence, the absence of any sourcing is a real weakness.
